title: smart-routing-fallback-incident-breadcrumbs-maya-chen
content:
TL;DR: During the 2026-02-24 02:10-02:40 UTC window we observed an increase in 503s from the realtime router when routing to eu-west-1 model pool. Smart routing attempted fallback to alternative regions, but the fallback chain was slower than expected and some requests hit the global rate limit and timed out. This doc is my personal breadcrumb log (commands, errors, hypotheses, quick tests, next steps).

Observed symptoms:
- Spike in 5xx (primarily 503/no healthy upstream) for requests targeting eu-west-1.
- Router logs show rapid failover attempts to us-west-2, us-east-1. Some fallbacks returned 200 but with high latency (>2.5s).
- Frontend clients reported timeouts (~10s). Error rate ~4.2% P95 10m.
- Related incident INC-2437 opened by oncall; escalation to infra at 02:30 UTC.

What I checked (commands & snippets):
1) Router pod logs (kubectl)
- cmd: kubectl -n inference logs deploy/realtime-router -c router --since=1h | grep "fallback" -n
- snippet: "[2026-02-24T02:12:11Z] router WARN fallback: route=embed-model-v2 src=eu-west-1 -> target=us-west-2 reason=instance_unhealthy"
- repeated lines showing `instance_unhealthy` and `connect_timeout`

2) Upstream health from control plane
- cmd: curl -sS http://control-plane.internal/api/pools/eu-west-1/health | jq '.'
- output: "{
  "pool": "eu-west-1",
  "healthy_instances": 2,
  "capacity_percent": 18
}"
- We normally expect ~8 healthy instances for that pool.

3) Node-level checks (on one affected GPU host)
- ssh to gpu-42.eu-west-1
- nvidia-smi: host shows 0/4 GPUs reporting (some driver instability)
- dmesg: saw repeated `NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:03:00): 79` errors ~02:05 UTC

4) Router metrics (Prometheus)
- Query: increase(router_request_failures_total{reason=~".*unhealthy.*"}[15m])
- result: spike starting 02:08 UTC, peaking 02:14 UTC
- fallback_latency_seconds histogram shows heavy tail: p95 ~1.9s, p99 ~3.4s for fallback requests

5) Redis (prefix cache / KV)
- redis-cli -h router-cache metrics: `used_memory_human: 12.3G` (close to max)
- cache hit ratio dropped from 94% -> 70% during window (evictions increased)
- hypothesis: more cache misses -> more cold starts to GPUs -> increased load on remaining instances

Error snippets collected:
- "503 Service Unavailable - no healthy upstream" (router log for ~800 requests)
- "timeout while waiting for headers" (client-facing LB)
- "NVRM: Xid 79: GPU has fallen off the bus" (kernel/dmesg on gpu hosts)
- "ERR max-clients reached" (redis occasionally reported during spike)

Short timeline (reconstructed):
- 02:03 UTC: first GPU errors reported in node telemetry (Xid 79).
- 02:06 UTC: control plane marks several instances in eu-west-1 as unhealthy (health-check failures).
- 02:08 UTC: Router starts failing requests to eu-west-1, triggers fallback to other regions.
- 02:10-02:20 UTC: fallback volume increases; fallback latency increases; redis cache pressure rises.
- 02:25 UTC: oncall escalates; mitigation attempts (drain suspicious nodes) start.
- 02:35 UTC: some nodes recovered; healthy_instance count slowly returns; errors taper off by 02:50 UTC.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Root: GPU driver/hardware problem in eu-west-1 caused instance health churn -> fallback overload. Evidence: NVRM Xid 79, nodes showing GPUs offline, control-plane health=2/expected 8.
2) Secondary: Router fallback policy serialized too aggressively to a small set of targets (sticky fallback) instead of spreading; caused hotspotting and pushed other regions near saturation. Evidence: metrics show fallback requests concentrated to us-west-2 cluster pool id=42 with higher queue length.
3) Tertiary: Cache pressure (redis evictions) amplified cold invocations across regions. Evidence: cache hit drop coincident with spike; redis max-clients warnings.
4) Edge-case: incorrect health-check timeout config made control-plane mark nodes unhealthy too quickly under transient driver errors.

Quick experiments / manual tests I ran (results):
- Manual replay of failing requests to router with --region hint:
  curl -X POST https://router.internal/v1/generate -d '{"region":"eu-west-1","model":"embed-v2","input":"test"}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer ...' -I
  -> 503 if eu-west-1 targeted; if no region hint router falls back to us-west-2 with 200 but latency ~2.6s.

- Adjusted fallback policy locally (non-prod cluster) to round-robin across fallback targets instead of priority list:
  -> p95 fallback latency reduced 15% in synthetic load tests. Suggests policy hot-spotting was real.

- Redis stress: connected to cache endpoint and ran INFO before/after synthetic load. Evictions jumped when fallback increased request fan-out.

Immediate mitigations applied during incident (by infra):
- Drained and rebooted affected GPU hosts (gpu-42..gpu-45).
- Temporarily increased fallback concurrency limit and added an extra fallback target in us-east-1 to spread load.
- Increased redis maxclients on router-cache from 10000 -> 15000 (quick patch).

Open questions / things to validate:
- Need to confirm root cause of Xid 79 on those hosts (driver version? kernel mismatch? recent kernel upgrades?) — request SRE to check node upgrade history and kernel-driver versions.
- Was the fallback policy change (round-robin vs priority) deployed recently? Check git history for router fallback config changes.
- Verify control-plane health-check thresholds: do we mark instances unhealthy too aggressively for transient Xid 79 bursts?
- Check autoscaling behavior for dedicated fallback pools: did autoscaler attempt to scale up and fail due to quota?

Next actions (priority order):
1) Postmortem skeleton (link to INC-2437) — capture timeline + root cause + mitigations. I'll draft initial timeline and hand to Ethan for metrics section.
2) File infra ticket to investigate GPU driver/kernel mismatch on eu-west-1 nodes and correlate with recent images (assign to @infra-sre).
3) Propose fallback policy change: adopt weighted round-robin with dynamic backoff for targets experiencing high queue length. Open PR: realtime-router/pull/421 already has a prototype; need review.
4) Increase cache capacity or tune eviction policy for router-cache; run resim tests to measure hit-rate impact.
5) Add better observability: add per-fallback-target queue length and per-request fallback_decision tag (so we can count which step in chain was used).

Notes to self: keep this short and messy — it's a scratchpad. Will expand into a cleaner postmortem and runbook after the infra investigation results. Reach out to Ethan and Riley to split the action items.

Raw log pointers (for digging):
- router logs: gs://redwood-logs/realtime-router/2026-02-24/02/*.log
- node telemetry: metrics.redwood.internal/nodes/eu-west-1/gpu-42/dmesg.txt
- prometheus queries: grafana.redwood.internal/d/abc123/router-fallback-overview

End of breadcrumbs (Maya)
